Neural Quantum States for Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy

Bharadwaj Chowdary Mummaneni Email: bharadwaj.chowdary.mummaneni@iao.fraunhofer.de Affiliation: Fraunhofer IAO, Nobelstraße 12, 70569 Stuttgart, Germany    Bo Xing Affiliation: Research Laboratory of Electronics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139, USA Affiliation: Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing (IAIC), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore 138632, Republic of Singapore
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Predicting a nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrum from first principles requires propagating a quantum state of dimension 2N2^{N} for NN coupled spins, which becomes intractable beyond larger NN. We benchmark Neural Quantum States (NQS), a class of variational quantum states expressed as an artificial neural network, as an alternative representation for this problem. Using two propagation methods, the Time-Dependent Variational Principle (TDVP) and projected time-dependent Variational Monte Carlo (p-tVMC), we compute the 1H spectra of four (2→52\to 5 spins) experimentally parameterized molecules. TDVP reproduces all line positions and intensities with average spectral mean squared errors of <10−3<10^{-3}; p-tVMC reproduces the same features, with accuracy determined by its per-step optimization parameters. One dominant obstacle to larger systems is the steep growth of the number of integration steps with spectral bandwidth, which can be removed by propagating in the interaction frame of the chemical-shifted Hamiltonian. Retaining the same accuracy, this reduces the number of integration steps roughly eightfold for the 3-spin system and by at least an order of magnitude for the 4- and 5-spin systems, and it enables a 14-spin molecule (sucrose) to be accurately propagated via Monte Carlo sampling.

I Introduction

When a chemist synthesizes a new compound or isolates a natural product, one of the first questions is whether the molecule in hand is actually the one intended. Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the standard tool for answering this question. Each chemically distinct nucleus resonates at a characteristic frequency, its chemical shift, and nuclei connected through chemical bonds interact via scalar couplings that split resonances into multiplet patterns. Together, these features encode the connectivity, stereochemistry, and conformation of the molecule [9, 25]. A proposed structure is confirmed when its predicted NMR spectrum matches the experimental one.

The first half of this prediction is now routine. Quantum-chemical methods, particularly Density Functional Theory (DFT), can compute NMR parameters (chemical shifts and JJ-couplings) from first principles [16, 27, 43], and programs such as Gaussian [11] and ORCA [29] can perform these calculations as a standard part of structure elucidation. However, to obtain the actual spectrum, one must propagate NN coupled spin-12\frac{1}{2} nuclei under the effective Hamiltonian and study the frequency domain of the time-domain signal: a quantum many-body time evolution in a Hilbert space of dimension 2N2^{N}, intractable beyond roughly N=15N=15–2020 [33]. Molecules with extended proton networks (natural products, peptides, polycyclic aromatics) routinely exceed this limit. Restricted state-space methods, implemented in the Spinach library, push the boundary considerably by discarding high-order spin correlations that remain essentially unpopulated in liquid-state experiments [24, 18], but their accuracy relies on truncation assumptions that must be validated for each coupling topology. Beyond the reach of these techniques, DFT-computed parameters cannot be turned into a spectrum, and the structural assignment remains incomplete.

Several strategies have been explored to overcome this exponential scaling. Nuclear spins map directly onto qubits [20, 26], but current quantum hardware does not yet provide the gate fidelities and coherence times that are useful for NMR simulation [32, 21, 10]. Tensor network methods compress the quantum state when the entanglement dynamics is not extensive [30, 42, 40], but their effectiveness for long-range and higher-dimensional Hamiltonians has not been systematically assessed. A third, largely unexplored alternative is Neural Quantum States (NQS): variational wavefunctions whose amplitudes are given by a neural network [5]. Initially proposed for finding the ground-state energy, NQS have since been extended to real-time dynamics through the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) [34, 44] and the projected time-dependent variational Monte Carlo (p-tVMC) method [35, 45]. NQS can represent certain classes of quantum states with only polynomially many parameters [12, 17, 31, 46], and their flexibility suits the complex coupling topologies that arise in NMR.

NMR poses a stringent test for any variational dynamics method. Unlike the ground-state energy, the quantity of interest is a frequency-domain response derived from a time-domain signal over the full simulation window, so even small phase errors accumulated during propagation appear as shifted or artificially broadened lines. Whether NQS can maintain the required accuracy over the hundreds to thousands of integration steps needed to resolve individual peaks can only be settled by direct numerical experiment.

In this work, we apply both TDVP and p-tVMC to four experimentally characterized 1H spin systems (2–5 coupled protons) and benchmark the resulting spectra against exact diagonalization. Both methods reproduce the correct line positions and intensities, with spectral mean squared errors of <10−3<10^{-3}, a proof of principle that NQS dynamics can compare DFT-computed parameters to experimentally obtained spectra. The principal bottleneck turns out to be the steep growth of the integration steps with system size and not neural network expressivity. We show that an exact transformation to the interacting frame can leave the spectrum unchanged reduces the steps needed at fixed accuracy roughly eightfold for the 3-spin system and by at least an order of magnitude for the 4- and 5-spin systems. This improvement in computation efficiency allows a 14-spin molecule (sucrose) to be propagated by Monte Carlo sampling.

II Theoretical Model

II.1 From FID to Spectrum

An NMR experiment records the free induction decay (FID): after a short radiofrequency pulse tips the equilibrium spin magnetization into the transverse plane, the sample coil picks up the oscillating voltage induced by the precessing nuclear spins. Each chemically distinct proton precesses at a slightly different frequency, its chemical shift δi\delta_{i} (in ppm), set by how strongly the surrounding electron cloud shields it from the applied field. Where two protons are connected by a few bonds, their magnetic moments interact through bonding electrons via the scalar coupling Ji​jJ_{ij} (in Hz), which splits each resonance into a multiplet. Fourier-transforming the FID converts this time-domain oscillation into the familiar spectrum of peaks, whose positions and splittings encode connectivity and conformation [3, 15].

To write the problem in a tractable form, NMR spectroscopists work in the rotating frame: a reference frame that co-rotates with the spins at the spectrometer frequency ν0=γ​B0/(2​π)\nu_{0}=\gamma B_{0}/(2\pi) (γ\gamma is the proton gyromagnetic ratio, B0B_{0} the static field). In this frame, the fast Larmor precession is removed, leaving only the slow, chemically informative differential precession between protons. The effective spin Hamiltonian is then [25, 1, 36]:

H^=∑i=1Nωi​I^z,i+2​π​∑i<jJi​j​𝐈^i⋅𝐈^j,\hat{H}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\omega_{i}\hat{I}_{z,i}+2\pi\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{j}, (1)

where 𝐈^i=(I^x,i,I^y,i,I^z,i)\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{i}=(\hat{I}_{x,i},\hat{I}_{y,i},\hat{I}_{z,i}) are the spin-12\frac{1}{2} operators of proton ii (eigenvalues ±12\pm\tfrac{1}{2}, in units of ℏ\hbar). The first term shifts each resonance to angular frequency ωi=2​π​ν0​(δi−δref)×10−6\omega_{i}=2\pi\nu_{0}(\delta_{i}-\delta_{\mathrm{ref}})\times 10^{-6} relative to the reference compound. The isotropic scalar coupling 2​π​Ji​j​𝐈^i⋅𝐈^j2\pi J_{ij}\,\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{j} (in rad/s, with Ji​jJ_{ij} reported in Hz) is the quantum-mechanical origin of multiplet splitting; its isotropic dot-product form holds for rapidly tumbling molecules in solution, where anisotropic dipolar couplings average to zero. Throughout this work we use B0=11.74 TB_{0}=$11.74\text{\,}\mathrm{T}$, giving ν0=500 MHz\nu_{0}=$500\text{\,}\mathrm{MHz}$.

After a 90y∘90^{\circ}_{y} pulse, the spin ensemble starts with all magnetization along xx. At high temperature the relevant part of the density matrix is proportional to I^xtot\hat{I}_{x}^{\mathrm{tot}}, and its time evolution gives the same spectral information as propagating the pure product state |ψ0⟩=|+x⟩⊗N\ket{\psi_0}=\ket{+_x}^{\otimes N}, with each proton initialized in the +x+x eigenstate, up to an overall normalization [25, 1]. The FID signal is the complex transverse magnetization:

S⁡(t)=⟨I^xtot​(t)⟩+i⁡⟨I^ytot​(t)⟩,S(t)=\langle\hat{I}_{x}^{\mathrm{tot}}(t)\rangle+i\,\langle\hat{I}_{y}^{\mathrm{tot}}(t)\rangle, (2)

with |Ψ⁡(t)⟩=e−i​H^​t​|ψ0⟩\ket{\Psi(t)}=e^{-i\hat{H}t}\ket{\psi_0} evolved under H^\hat{H}. The spectrum follows from a Fourier transform with an exponential window [23, 9]:

S⁡(ω)=∫0TS⁡(t)​e−λ​t​e−i​ω​t​𝑑t.S(\omega)=\int_{0}^{T}S(t)\,e^{-\lambda t}\,e^{-i\omega t}\,dt. (3)

The apodization factor e−λ​te^{-\lambda t} mimics the T2∗T_{2}^{*} decay that broadens experimental lines (we use λ=3.0 s−1\lambda=$3.0\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$, giving ∼1 Hz\sim$1\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$ Lorentzian linewidth) and damps ringing from the finite acquisition window TT. The computational task is therefore to propagate |Ψ⁡(t)⟩\ket{\Psi(t)} faithfully over T=1.0 sT=$1.0\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ and evaluate S⁡(t)S(t) at each timestep: a quantum dynamics problem whose cost grows as 2N2^{N} with the number of coupled protons NN.

II.2 Interaction-Frame Propagation

The rotating-frame Hamiltonian of Eq. (1) contains two terms separated by orders of magnitude in energy. The one-body chemical-shift term H^0=∑iωi​I^z,i\hat{H}_{0}=\sum_{i}\omega_{i}\hat{I}_{z,i} has matrix elements of order 10210^{2}–10310^{3} rad/s, while the scalar coupling H^1=2​π​∑i<jJi​j​𝐈^i⋅𝐈^j\hat{H}_{1}=2\pi\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{j} is of order 10110^{1} rad/s. An explicit integrator must resolve the fastest oscillation present in the propagated state, so the chemical-shift precession (though spectroscopically a trivial single-spin phase e−i​ωi​te^{-i\omega_{i}t}) sets the usable timestep and is responsible for the steep growth in step count reported in Table 1. This is numerical stiffness in the standard sense: the step size is dictated by the fastest frequency present rather than by the slower dynamics of interest. We quantify it by the offset-to-coupling ratio maxi​j⁡|ωi−ωj|/2​π​Ji​j\max_{ij}|\omega_{i}-\omega_{j}|/2\pi J_{ij}.

This stiffness can be removed analytically by propagating in the interaction frame of H^0\hat{H}_{0}. Writing U^0​(t)=ei​H^0​t\hat{U}_{0}(t)=e^{i\hat{H}_{0}t} and |ΨI​(t)⟩=U^0​(t)​|Ψ⁡(t)⟩\ket{\Psi_I(t)}=\hat{U}_{0}(t)\ket{\Psi(t)}, the transformed state obeys i​∂t|ΨI⟩=H^I​(t)​|ΨI⟩i\partial_{t}\ket{\Psi_I}=\hat{H}_{I}(t)\ket{\Psi_I} with a generator that retains only the coupling, dressed by phases oscillating at the chemical-shift differences:

H^I(t)=2π∑i<jJi​j[I^z,iI^z,j+12(ei⁡(ωi−ωj)​tI^+(i)I^−(j)+h.c.)].\hat{H}_{I}(t)=2\pi\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\Big[\hat{I}_{z,i}\hat{I}_{z,j}+\tfrac{1}{2}\big(e^{i(\omega_{i}-\omega_{j})t}\,\hat{I}_{+}^{(i)}\hat{I}_{-}^{(j)}+\mathrm{h.c.}\big)\Big]. (4)

The large one-body term has vanished from the generator; what remains has magnitude ∼2​π​Ji​j\sim 2\pi J_{ij}, the slow coupling scale. The price is that H^I​(t)\hat{H}_{I}(t) is explicitly time dependent, with off-diagonal elements oscillating at the chemical-shift differences. This is a good trade: the rate at which the state changes is bounded by the norm of the generator, not by how rapidly its phases oscillate, so |ΨI​(t)⟩\ket{\Psi_I(t)} moves on the slow coupling timescale and the integrator can take correspondingly larger steps.

The transformation is the standard interaction (Dirac) picture of quantum mechanics and involves no approximation: |Ψ⁡(t)⟩=U^0†​(t)​|ΨI​(t)⟩\ket{\Psi(t)}=\hat{U}_{0}^{\dagger}(t)\ket{\Psi_I(t)} reproduces the rotating-frame state exactly at every instant. In particular, the chemical shifts are not discarded; they are applied analytically rather than integrated numerically. The laboratory-frame signal follows by transforming back,

⟨I^+tot​(t)⟩=∑kei​ωk​t​⟨ΨI|​I^+(k)​|ΨI⟩.\langle\hat{I}_{+}^{\mathrm{tot}}(t)\rangle=\sum_{k}e^{i\omega_{k}t}\,\bra{\Psi_I}\hat{I}_{+}^{(k)}\ket{\Psi_I}. (5)

Each factor ei​ωk​te^{i\omega_{k}t} is precisely the offset precession of spin kk; in the frequency domain it translates the multiplet of that spin, which the interaction-frame dynamics generates around zero frequency, to its chemical-shift position ωk\omega_{k}. Peak positions are thus restored exactly by the analytic phases, while the multiplet structure is carried by the propagated coupling dynamics. The resulting spectrum is identical to the rotating-frame one; only the numerical cost differs, because the integrator no longer resolves single-spin precession that is known in closed form.

II.3 Molecular Spin Systems

We study four molecules of increasing spectral complexity (Fig. 1), chosen to cover a range of coupling topologies representative of common organic structural motifs:

  • •

    2-spin: cis-3-Chloroacrylic acid. The two vinyl protons are coupled by a single vicinal J3{}^{3}J constant, producing a simple doublet, the minimal non-trivial NMR pattern.

  • •

    3-spin: 1,2,4-Trichlorobenzene. Three aromatic protons at the 3-, 5-, and 6-positions are magnetically inequivalent and carry different JJ couplings, giving an ABX-type multiplet structure.

  • •

    4-spin: 3-Methyleneoxetan-2-one. The exocyclic methylene and ring protons form a tightly coupled four-spin system with several overlapping multiplets.

  • •

    5-spin: Nitrobenzene. The five aromatic protons split into ortho, meta, and para sets by molecular symmetry; their coupling pattern is a textbook example of monosubstituted-benzene multiplet structure.

Hamiltonian parameters (chemical shifts and JJ-couplings) are taken from experimental databases [7, 19]. For each system, the exact reference spectrum is computed by dense matrix exponentiation of H^\hat{H}. For the interaction-frame comparison (Table 2) we additionally include sucrose (N=14N=14), a disaccharide with fourteen inequivalent protons. Its JJ-coupling network splits into three disconnected groups of 7, 5, and 2 protons, so it is a comparatively benign large system rather than a strongly correlated one; we quantify this in Sec. IV.2. Its exact reference is obtained by sparse Krylov propagation (expm_multiply) rather than dense diagonalization, and the NQS never enumerates its 2142^{14}-dimensional Hilbert space.

III Computational Methods

III.1 Neural Quantum State Representation

We represent the instantaneous quantum state using a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM), a two-layer neural network comprising visible units (corresponding to the NN physical spins) and M=α​NM=\alpha N hidden units. The wavefunction amplitude for a spin configuration 𝐬=(s1,…,sN)∈{−1,+1}N\mathbf{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{N})\in\{-1,+1\}^{N} takes the form [5, 2]:

ψ⁡(𝐬)=e∑iai​si​∏j=1M2​cosh⁡(bj+∑iWj​i​si),\psi(\mathbf{s})=e^{\sum_{i}a_{i}s_{i}}\prod_{j=1}^{M}2\cosh\left(b_{j}+\sum_{i}W_{ji}s_{i}\right), (6)

where {ai}∈ℂN\{a_{i}\}\in\mathbb{C}^{N}, {bj}∈ℂM\{b_{j}\}\in\mathbb{C}^{M}, and W∈ℂM×NW\in\mathbb{C}^{M\times N} are variational parameters. The hidden unit ratio α\alpha controls the network’s expressive capacity.

The RBM is attractive here because the hidden units can be summed out analytically, giving ψ⁡(𝐬)\psi(\mathbf{s}) in 𝒪⁡(α​N2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha N^{2}) operations. Complex-valued parameters are needed to capture the phases that develop during unitary evolution [34]. For states with limited entanglement, the required number of hidden units scales polynomially [12], but volume-law entangled states may demand exponentially many. It is not known a priori which regime NMR time evolution falls into.

III.2 Time-Dependent Variational Principle

Exact time evolution under H^\hat{H} generates a trajectory |Ψ⁡(t)⟩=e−i​H^​t​|Ψ⁡(0)⟩\ket{\Psi(t)}=e^{-i\hat{H}t}\ket{\Psi(0)} through the full 2N2^{N}-dimensional Hilbert space. The NQS ansatz restricts the state to the variational manifold ℳ={|Ψ⁡(𝜽)⟩:𝜽∈ℂP}\mathcal{M}=\{\ket{\Psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})}:\bm{\theta}\in\mathbb{C}^{P}\}, and TDVP [28, 14, 44] provides the optimal equations of motion for the parameters 𝜽⁡(t)\bm{\theta}(t) on this manifold.

We project the Schrödinger equation ∂t|Ψ⟩=−i​H^​|Ψ⟩\partial_{t}\ket{\Psi}=-i\hat{H}\ket{\Psi} onto the tangent space T𝜽​ℳT_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{M}, spanned by {|∂μΨ⟩}\{\ket{\partial_\mu\Psi}\}. The time derivatives θ˙μ\dot{\theta}_{\mu} are chosen so that the resulting state update, ∂t|Ψ⁡(𝜽)⟩=∑μθ˙μ​|∂μΨ⟩\partial_{t}\ket{\Psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})}=\sum_{\mu}\dot{\theta}_{\mu}\ket{\partial_\mu\Psi}, is as close as possible, in the Hilbert-space norm, to the exact right-hand side −i​H^​|Ψ⟩-i\hat{H}\ket{\Psi}. This least-squares condition reads:

min𝜽˙⁡‖∑μθ˙μ​|∂μΨ⟩+i​H^​|Ψ⟩‖2,\min_{\dot{\bm{\theta}}}\left\|\sum_{\mu}\dot{\theta}_{\mu}\ket{\partial_\mu\Psi}+i\hat{H}\ket{\Psi}\right\|^{2}, (7)

whose solution is the linear system of equations of motion [34]:

𝐒​𝜽˙=−i​𝐅.\mathbf{S}\,\dot{\bm{\theta}}=-i\,\mathbf{F}. (8)

Both 𝐒\mathbf{S} and 𝐅\mathbf{F} are estimated stochastically from nsamplesn_{\mathrm{samples}} configurations drawn from the Born distribution |ψ⁡(𝐬)|2|\psi(\mathbf{s})|^{2}. Defining the log-derivative Oμ​(𝐬)=∂θμln⁡ψ⁡(𝐬)O_{\mu}(\mathbf{s})=\partial_{\theta_{\mu}}\ln\psi(\mathbf{s}) and the local energy Eloc​(𝐬)=∑𝐬′⟨𝐬|H^|𝐬′⟩​ψ​(𝐬′)/ψ⁡(𝐬)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s})=\sum_{\mathbf{s}^{\prime}}\langle\mathbf{s}|\hat{H}|\mathbf{s}^{\prime}\rangle\psi(\mathbf{s}^{\prime})/\psi(\mathbf{s}), the quantum geometric tensor (quantum Fisher information matrix) [37, 38] and the force vector are the connected covariances:

Sμ​ν\displaystyle S_{\mu\nu} =⟨Oμ∗​Oν⟩c,\displaystyle=\langle O_{\mu}^{*}O_{\nu}\rangle_{c}, (9)
Fμ\displaystyle F_{\mu} =⟨Oμ∗​Eloc⟩c,\displaystyle=\langle O_{\mu}^{*}E_{\mathrm{loc}}\rangle_{c}, (10)

where ⟨A​B⟩c≡⟨A​B⟩−⟨A⟩​⟨B⟩\langle AB\rangle_{c}\equiv\langle AB\rangle-\langle A\rangle\langle B\rangle denotes the connected expectation value. Sμ​νS_{\mu\nu} measures how independently different parameters deform the quantum state (it is the Gram matrix of the tangent vectors in the Fubini–Study metric); 𝐅\mathbf{F} measures how much each parameter direction overlaps with the exact Schrödinger drive −i​H^​|Ψ⟩-i\hat{H}\ket{\Psi}. These equations of motion are reparameterization-covariant: the physical trajectory is independent of how the network is parameterized, and the method reduces to natural gradient descent in the geometry of quantum state space [38, 13].

III.3 Projected Time-Dependent Variational Monte Carlo

The projected time-dependent Variational Monte Carlo (p-tVMC) method [35] takes a different approach from TDVP: rather than integrating a differential equation on ℳ\mathcal{M}, it advances the state by projecting the exactly evolved quantum state back onto the variational manifold at each discrete timestep. Concretely, after applying the exact propagator for one step, the target state is

|Φt⟩=e−i​H^​Δ​t​|Ψ⁡(𝜽t)⟩,\ket{\Phi_t}=e^{-i\hat{H}\Delta t}\ket{\Psi(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)}, (11)

which in general lies outside ℳ\mathcal{M}. The projection finds the variational state |Ψ⁡(𝜽t+1)⟩∈ℳ\ket{\Psi(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1})}\in\mathcal{M} closest to |Φt⟩\ket{\Phi_t} by minimizing the quantum infidelity:

ℐ⁡(𝜽)=1−|⟨Ψ⁡(𝜽)|Φt⟩|2⟨Ψ⁡(𝜽)|Ψ⁡(𝜽)⟩​⟨Φt|Φt⟩.\mathcal{I}(\bm{\theta})=1-\frac{|\innerproduct{\Psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\Phi_t}|^{2}}{\innerproduct{\Psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\Psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\innerproduct{\Phi_t}{\Phi_t}}. (12)

ℐ=0\mathcal{I}=0 means perfect overlap (the variational ansatz can represent the propagated state exactly); ℐ=1\mathcal{I}=1 means the two states are orthogonal.

In our implementation, the exact propagator e−i​H^​Δ​te^{-i\hat{H}\Delta t} is precomputed once as a dense 2N×2N2^{N}\times 2^{N} matrix via matrix exponentiation and cached throughout the simulation; this is feasible for N≤12N\leq 12 and eliminates propagator discretization errors from the benchmark. The infidelity ℐ\mathcal{I} and its gradient are estimated by Monte Carlo: configurations 𝝈\bm{\sigma} are sampled from |ψ𝜽​(𝝈)|2|\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})|^{2} and independently 𝜼\bm{\eta} from |ϕt​(𝜼)|2|\phi_{t}(\bm{\eta})|^{2}. The key estimator is

Iloc​(𝝈,𝜼)=ϕt​(𝝈)ψ𝜽​(𝝈)⋅ψ𝜽​(𝜼)ϕt​(𝜼),ℐ=1−|⟨Iloc⟩|2,I_{\mathrm{loc}}(\bm{\sigma},\bm{\eta})=\frac{\phi_{t}(\bm{\sigma})}{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})}\cdot\frac{\psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\eta})}{\phi_{t}(\bm{\eta})},\quad\mathcal{I}=1-|\langle I_{\mathrm{loc}}\rangle|^{2}, (13)

where each factor is the amplitude ratio of the two wavefunctions at a sampled configuration; together they form an importance-sampled estimator of the squared overlap |⟨Ψ⁡(𝜽)|Φt⟩|2|\langle\Psi(\bm{\theta})|\Phi_{t}\rangle|^{2}. Gradient variance is reduced by the control variate [35]

IlocCV=Re⁡{Iloc}−c⁡(|1−Iloc|2−1),I_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{CV}}=\mathrm{Re}\{I_{\mathrm{loc}}\}-c\!\left(|1-I_{\mathrm{loc}}|^{2}-1\right), (14)

with c=−1/2c=-1/2 optimal for small infidelities. Gradients are computed by automatic differentiation and passed to the Adam optimizer [22]; optionally, Stochastic Reconfiguration (SR) preconditioning can be applied to the updates.

Compared with TDVP, p-tVMC sidesteps QGT inversion, and the per-step ℐ\mathcal{I} gives a running diagnostic of how well the variational manifold tracks the true evolution. The per-step cost 𝒪⁡(niter⋅nsamples⋅P)\mathcal{O}(n_{\mathrm{iter}}\cdot n_{\mathrm{samples}}\cdot P) exceeds the 𝒪⁡(nsamples⋅P2)\mathcal{O}(n_{\mathrm{samples}}\cdot P^{2}) of TDVP, but iterative optimization avoids the regularization bias that accumulates in TDVP. For N≳12N\gtrsim 12, the dense propagator must be replaced by a Trotter–Suzuki decomposition; this introduces an 𝒪⁡(Δ​t2)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{2}) Trotter error per step and is the main scalability bottleneck of the current implementation.

III.4 Implementation

We implement both the NQS-TDVP and p-tVMC methods using NetKet [39], an open-source library built on JAX that provides automatic differentiation, just-in-time compilation, and GPU acceleration. The variational state employs Metropolis-Hastings sampling with local spin-flip proposals, using nsamples=4096n_{\mathrm{samples}}=4096 configurations per time step. This is admittedly excessive for the N≤5N\leq 5 systems, where exact summation over all basis configurations is possible; we keep Monte Carlo sampling rather than exact summation throughout, to stay true to the larger systems for which the method is meant, where summing over all configurations is out of reach. All benchmarks were run on a single CPU node using 8 threads (Intel Xeon, 2.4 GHz2.4\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}); the wall times reported in Table 1 refer to this configuration. For direct method comparison, both TDVP and p-tVMC use the same hidden unit ratio α=4\alpha=4. For the TDVP-only scaling results in Table 1, we additionally identified α\alpha that minimizes the spectral MSE for each system. The MSE is computed over the spectral region containing peaks after normalizing both the NQS and the exact spectra to the unit maximum.

TDVP integration: Time propagation uses the Heun method (second-order Runge-Kutta) with timestep Δ​t\Delta t, and the linear system 𝐒⋅Δ​𝜽=−i​𝐅​Δ​t\mathbf{S}\cdot\Delta\bm{\theta}=-i\,\mathbf{F}\,\Delta t is solved via singular value decomposition with diagonal regularization ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01 for numerical stability. For each system we vary Δ​t\Delta t over four to five values, keeping the total simulation time fixed at T=1.0 sT=$1.0\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$, and use the value that minimizes the spectral MSE; the scanned ranges run from 0.10.1–0.0050.005 s for the 2-spin system down to 10−310^{-3}–10−410^{-4} s for the 5-spin system, and the optima are listed in Table 1.

p-tVMC optimization: The exact propagator U⁡(Δ​t)=e−i​H^​Δ​tU(\Delta t)=e^{-i\hat{H}\Delta t} is precomputed once as a dense 2N×2N2^{N}\times 2^{N} matrix via matrix exponentiation and cached throughout the simulation. At each time step, the infidelity ℐ\mathcal{I} is minimized using the Adam optimizer [22] with learning rate η=0.01\eta=0.01 and niter=50n_{\mathrm{iter}}=50 gradient updates per step. The control variate coefficient is c=−0.5c=-0.5. An optional Stochastic Reconfiguration preconditioner (diagonal shift ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01) was tested but not found to improve results consistently.

The RBM parameters are initialized with small random values (scale =0.01=0.01, seed =42=42). Because the product state |+x⟩⊗N\ket{+_x}^{\otimes N} can be represented exactly by an RBM, convergence to the correct initial state is verified by checking that ⟨I^xtot⟩=N/2\langle\hat{I}_{x}^{\mathrm{tot}}\rangle=N/2 to within statistical error before beginning time propagation. Molecular Hamiltonian parameters (chemical shifts and JJ-couplings) are taken from experimental databases [7, 19].

IV Results

IV.1 Rotating-Frame Benchmarks

We begin with the 2-spin system, where the dynamics can be visualized directly. Figure 2 shows the transverse magnetization ⟨I^x​(t)⟩\langle\hat{I}_{x}(t)\rangle over the full T=1.0 sT=$1.0\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ window at successive integration timesteps. The beating pattern is the time-domain signature of the doublet: two precessing frequencies that alternately reinforce and cancel. At coarse Δ​t=0.1\Delta t=0.1 s (10 steps) both TDVP and p-tVMC drift from the exact solution in amplitude and phase. By Δ​t=0.005\Delta t=0.005 s (Nt=200N_{t}=200) the TDVP curve is indistinguishable from the exact, and p-tVMC tracks it closely, though with larger residual error (quantified below). The exponential window e−λ​te^{-\lambda t} downweights the late-time signal, where errors accumulate most, so the spectral accuracy is somewhat better than the raw time-domain discrepancy suggests.

The spectral consequences are shown in Fig. 3 for all four molecules. Each panel stacks the NQS spectra at successive Δ​t\Delta t values (coarsest at top, finest at bottom), with p-tVMC in green and the exact reference as dashed black. For the 2-spin doublet of cis-3-chloroacrylic acid, line positions are resolved already at Nt=20N_{t}=20 steps; the fine splitting and clean baseline emerge only at Nt=200N_{t}=200. The ABX multiplet of 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene (6.8–7.8 ppm) sharpens progressively with smaller Δ​t\Delta t, though low-intensity oscillations between peaks persist at intermediate step counts. The four-spin system shows noisier baselines, consistent with the higher initialization sensitivity discussed below, but reproduces the correct multiplet pattern at fine Δ​t\Delta t. Nitrobenzene, with its ortho/meta/para sub-patterns, requires Nt=10,000N_{t}=10{,}000 steps, fifty times more than the 2-spin case: much finer spectral structure must be resolved over the same 1 s window. In every case, the simulated spectra converge toward the exact reference as Δ​t\Delta t decreases.

Table 1 and Fig. 4 quantify the computational cost across all four systems (MSE averaged over 5 random seeds). The required Δ​t\Delta t shrinks with NN, tracking the growing spectral bandwidth of larger spin systems. MSE does not increase monotonically: the 4-spin molecule achieves lower mean error than 3-spin, and the 5-spin the lowest of all, reflecting genuine differences in spectral complexity between molecules. Initialization sensitivity tells a different story: the coefficient of variation grows from 3% at N=2N=2 to 32% at N=4N=4, so single-seed results can be misleading. In general, we expect spectral MSE to decrease as the network size increases, and this is reflected in the 2−2-, 3−3-, 5−5-spin systems. For the 4-spin system, the best accuracy is at α=1\alpha=1. This anomaly could have arisen from chance, such as obtaining more favorable initialization seeds, or having specific coupling parameters. Repeating the sweep on a different 4-spin molecule would distinguish the two.

The two methods handle the computation-accuracy tradeoff differently. TDVP solves the linear system 𝐒​𝜽˙=−i​𝐅\mathbf{S}\,\dot{\bm{\theta}}=-i\mathbf{F} once per step at a cost that is fixed for given nsamplesn_{\mathrm{samples}} and α\alpha. p-tVMC instead runs nitern_{\mathrm{iter}} gradient steps per timestep (niter=50n_{\mathrm{iter}}=50 for the spectra in Fig. 3, α=4\alpha=4). Across the four systems it reaches spectral MSEs between 2.6×10−32.6\times 10^{-3} (5-spin, run at niter=75n_{\mathrm{iter}}=75) and 3.7×10−23.7\times 10^{-2} (3-spin), with per-step infidelities of 10−510^{-5}–10−210^{-2}. These errors are higher than the TDVP optima in Table 1, though the comparison is not direct since TDVP used the molecule-specific optimal α\alpha while p-tVMC used α=4\alpha=4 throughout. Figure 5 shows the iteration sweep for the 2-spin system: as nitern_{\mathrm{iter}} increases from 10 to 100, wall time grows from ∼80{\sim}80 s to ∼670{\sim}670 s while MSE drops by nearly four orders of magnitude. The improvement is still monotonic at niter=100n_{\mathrm{iter}}=100, confirming that accuracy at these system sizes is limited by optimizer budget rather than network expressivity.

IV.2 Effect of the Interaction Frame

Most of the integration steps in Table 1 are spent resolving the chemical-shift term rather than the couplings that carry the spectral information. Since the interaction-frame transformation of Eq. (4) removes that term exactly, we used it to ask how much of the cost it accounts for. Because interaction frame transformation operator U^0​(t)\hat{U}_{0}(t) is diagonal and a product of single-spin zz-rotations, applying it costs nothing and leaves the entanglement structure, and hence the RBM representability, of the state unchanged; for the ansatz of Eq. (6) it is absorbed exactly into a drift of the complex visible biases, ai​(t)=ai​(0)−i⁡(ωi/2)​ta_{i}(t)=a_{i}(0)-i(\omega_{i}/2)\,t. We repeated the TDVP propagation in both frames under otherwise identical settings: RBM with α=4\alpha=4 for the N≤5N\leq 5 molecules and α=2\alpha=2 for the N=14N=14 sucrose, 40964096 samples per step, and the same Heun integrator, QGT/SVD solver, and sampler. The rotating frame was pushed to NtN_{t} as large as 10410^{4} to follow its convergence. Figure 6 shows the spectral MSE against the number of steps NtN_{t} in both frames, and Table 2 summarizes the contrast.

These runs are a controlled frame comparison at fixed network size, not accuracy-optimized, so their rotating-frame errors exceed the Table 1 values at the same NN, which used the molecule-specific αopt\alpha_{\mathrm{opt}} and timestep averaged over five seeds. Repeating the 4- and 5-spin comparison at α=2\alpha=2 leaves the picture unchanged (rotating frame at 11–2×10−22\times 10^{-2} at Nt=3200N_{t}=3200, interaction frame at its floor), so the contrast is not an artifact of the network size.

The size of the effect depends strongly on the molecule. For the 2-spin system, the two frames are equivalent, as expected: the chemical-shift evolution is a time-linear shift of the RBM visible biases (Sec. II.2), which the integrator reproduces exactly, so there is nothing to remove. For the 3-spin molecule, where the rotating frame still reaches the target accuracy, the interaction frame attains MSE <10−3<10^{-3} in about 200200 steps rather than roughly 16001600 (three seeds; one remains marginally above 10−310^{-3} at Nt=1600N_{t}=1600), an approximately eightfold reduction at fixed accuracy.

For the 4- and 5-spin molecules, the contrast is larger. The interaction frame drops below MSE 10−310^{-3} within a few hundred steps (Nt≈200N_{t}\approx 200 and ≈800\approx 800, respectively) and then flattens at an NtN_{t}-independent residual of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6} and 1.7×10−41.7\times 10^{-4}, respectively: an error floor set by sampling noise and the QGT regularization rather than by the time step. The rotating frame instead needs of order 10310^{3}–10410^{4} steps: pushed to the largest step counts we ran, its error keeps decreasing, reaching 7.1×10−37.1\times 10^{-3} at Nt=8000N_{t}=8000 (4-spin, convergence-run seed) and (1.7±0.4)×10−3(1.7\pm 0.4)\times 10^{-3} at Nt=104N_{t}=10^{4} (5-spin, three seeds) (Fig. 6). This points to slow stiffness rather than a hard error floor: the rotating frame converges toward the same spectrum, but the large chemical-shift term forces a small time step. Individual seeds are not monotonic, however. At intermediate NtN_{t} the rotating-frame error scatters strongly across seeds and reruns (at Nt=3200N_{t}=3200 for the 4-spin system, four runs span 1.21.2–3.1×10−23.1\times 10^{-2}); we read this as sampling noise riding on a slowly decreasing signal, not as a plateau.

The advantage survives in wall-clock time. For the 4- and 5-spin systems, the interaction frame, whose dressed coupling generator is rebuilt at every step, costs 1010–40%40\% more per step. The 4-spin system nevertheless reached MSE ≈5×10−6\approx 5\times 10^{-6} in ≈450 s{\approx}\,$450\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ (Nt=1600N_{t}=1600), whereas the rotating frame was still at 7×10−37\times 10^{-3} after ≈2050 s{\approx}\,$2050\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$ (Nt=8000N_{t}=8000). Removing the large one-body term also reduces the magnitude of the force 𝐅=⟨O∗​Eloc⟩\mathbf{F}=\langle O^{*}E_{\mathrm{loc}}\rangle, and with it the bias from the QGT diagonal shift; consistent with this, the interaction-frame results were markedly more reproducible across seeds (spreads below 10%10\%) than the rotating-frame ones.

Sucrose (N=14N=14) probes a larger system, sampled by Monte Carlo rather than full enumeration. Within the Nt≤800N_{t}\leq 800 steps we ran, the interaction frame reaches MSE ∼6×10−5{\sim}6\times 10^{-5} while the rotating frame is still at ∼2×10−2{\sim}2\times 10^{-2} (one of three seeds reached 4×10−34\times 10^{-3}); we did not push the rotating frame to convergence and quote sucrose only as a feasibility point.

The successful simulation of the 14-proton molecule points works in favor of NQ. The successful run at N=14N=14 is concrete evidence that the approach extends well beyond the few-spin benchmarks. We further highlight that a larger molecule is not necessarily a harder one. Figure 7 shows the bipartite von Neumann entanglement entropy of the exact state along the trajectory, maximized (“worst cut”) and minimized (“best cut”) over balanced bipartitions. The 4- and 5-spin molecules entangle across every balanced cut, with the worst approaching the maximal 22 bits. Sucrose does not: its JJ-coupling network splits into three disconnected clusters (7, 5, and 2 protons), so the problem factorizes into independent blocks and becomes easier than its size suggests, its cost set by the largest block of 7 spins rather than by all 14. In this case, the coupling structure can further simplify molecules. More broadly, the appeal of NQS for larger systems is that, unlike tensor networks, they are not bounded by connectivity or entanglement across a cut [8]. They can remain efficient as that entanglement grows.

Two caveats bound this comparison. First, both frames used the same second-order integrator; a higher-order or adaptive scheme would also shorten the rotating-frame calculation, so the interaction frame is a cheap and exact way to handle the chemical-shift contribution, not the only one. Second, for the N≤5N\leq 5 molecules, the 40964096 samples far exceed the Hilbert-space dimension (≤32\leq 32), so those comparisons are effectively at the exact-summation limit. Sucrose is the only genuine test of sparse stochastic sampling (40964096 samples in a 214=163842^{14}=16384-dimensional space); the low MSE reached there is an encouraging first data point rather than a systematic study of how accuracy scales with sample count, and the behaviour of larger, more strongly correlated systems, where entanglement rather than the chemical shift dominates the cost, remains open.

V Discussion

V.1 Method Comparison and Error Budget

TDVP is cheaper per step and works well when the QGT stays well-conditioned; p-tVMC is more expensive but gives a per-step error diagnostic (the infidelity) and avoids QGT inversion entirely. At larger system sizes, the infidelity could serve as an adaptive convergence criterion, allocating fewer optimization iterations when the variational manifold tracks the true evolution closely and more when it does not. TDVP has no comparable built-in quality indicator, and its per-step cost is fixed regardless of local approximation quality.

The spectral error has four contributions, whose relative importance differs between the two methods. (i) Integration/projection error. The Heun integrator used in TDVP has 𝒪⁡(Δ​t3)\mathcal{O}(\Delta t^{3}) local truncation error, giving 𝒪⁡(T​Δ​t2)\mathcal{O}(T\Delta t^{2}) global error; higher-order integrators would reduce this. In p-tVMC, the analogous quantity is the residual infidelity per step. (ii) Statistical noise. Finite sampling (nsamples=4096n_{\mathrm{samples}}=4096) introduces fluctuations in the QGT and forces (TDVP) or the infidelity gradient (p-tVMC), with standard errors of ∼ 1.5%{\sim}\,1.5\% of mean values [6]. (iii) QGT regularization (TDVP only). The diagonal shift ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01 biases the equations of motion; reducing ϵ\epsilon helps but amplifies sampling noise. p-tVMC avoids this trade-off. (iv) Variational expressivity. If the true state develops entanglement that the RBM cannot efficiently represent, both methods will drift from the exact trajectory; this is the most fundamental limitation.

V.2 Implications for Practical NMR Simulation

For 2–5 spins, exact diagonalization is trivially faster (the largest Hilbert space here is 25=322^{5}=32); the point of the benchmark is to characterize how NQS accuracy and cost scale before reaching sizes where exact methods fail. Exact propagation scales as 𝒪⁡(2N)\mathcal{O}(2^{N}) in memory and 𝒪⁡(22​N)\mathcal{O}(2^{2N}) per matrix-vector product, while NQS-TDVP requires 𝒪⁡(α​N2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha N^{2}) parameters and 𝒪⁡(nsamples⋅α​N2)\mathcal{O}(n_{\mathrm{samples}}\cdot\alpha N^{2}) per step (p-tVMC multiplies this by nitern_{\mathrm{iter}}). From four data points, the number of required timesteps clearly grows faster than linearly in NN, but the functional form cannot be pinned down; if α\alpha stays moderate, the crossover should occur around N≈15N\approx 15–20. A head-to-head benchmark against restricted state-space methods [18] on identical molecules would establish where, if anywhere, NQS offer a genuine advantage over the best classical alternatives.

Liquid-state NMR spectra of medium-sized organic molecules involve >>20 coupled protons; proteins can have >>100. Our 2–5 spin benchmarks do not reach those scales, but two observations are relevant.

The correlation-function route to the spectrum (time-propagate, record ⟨I^+​(t)⟩\langle\hat{I}_{+}(t)\rangle, Fourier-transform) works straightforwardly with NQS dynamics. The MSE values in Table 1 (10−410^{-4}–10−310^{-3}) correspond to spectral distortions well below typical experimental linewidths (∼1 Hz{\sim}\,$1\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}$), so the accuracy would be sufficient if it persists at larger NN.

The bottleneck is cost. The number of integration steps grows steeply with NN, and much of it is spent on the chemical-shift term rather than on the couplings. Removing that term by the interaction-frame transformation (Sec. II.2) recovers a useful fraction of the cost (about eightfold for the 3-spin molecule) and improves the seed-to-seed reproducibility of the larger cases, without changing the spectrum. This addresses only the chemical-shift contribution, however; the cost of representing and integrating strongly entangled states, which we expect to dominate for larger and more densely coupled molecules, is unaffected.

V.3 Open Questions

The key open question is how entanglement grows with the size of the largest connected coupling cluster. For the molecules studied here, the entanglement within any connected cluster stays at a few bits (Fig. 7), but a molecule with 10–20 protons in a single connected network could push the state toward a volume-law regime where exponentially many hidden units are needed. Characterizing that growth would clarify whether RBMs remain the right ansatz or whether transformer-based [41] or autoregressive [17] architectures, which have outperformed RBMs in some ground-state problems, are needed for dynamics as well.

Real NMR experiments also include T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} relaxation, which damp high-frequency oscillations and shorten the effective simulation window. Incorporating Lindblad dynamics [4] might reduce the number of timesteps needed while making the simulation more physically realistic.

VI Conclusions

For 2–5 spin molecular systems, NQS with an RBM ansatz reproduces 1H NMR spectra to spectral MSE of 10−410^{-4}–10−310^{-3} at optimal parameters (Table 1), using both TDVP and p-tVMC propagation. Multi-seed statistics show that initialization sensitivity varies strongly between systems (coefficient of variation from 3% at N=2N=2 to 32% at N=4N=4), so reporting single-seed results can be misleading.

At these system sizes, the main finding is that the bottleneck is not network expressivity or memory, but the steep growth in required integration steps with NN. RBMs with α≤10\alpha\leq 10 have sufficient representational capacity; what limits accuracy is the accumulation of variational and integration error over thousands of propagation steps. p-tVMC avoids the ill-conditioning issues of QGT inversion and provides a per-step error diagnostic, but at 1010–20×20{\times} the wall-clock cost of TDVP.

Part of the timestep cost can be removed for free by propagating in the interaction frame of the chemical-shift Hamiltonian, an exact transformation that leaves the spectrum unchanged. In our tests, this cut the steps needed at fixed accuracy roughly eightfold for the 3-spin molecule and by at least an order of magnitude for the 4- and 5-spin systems (Table 2), and allowed a 14-spin molecule to be propagated by sampling; the interaction-frame results were reproducible across random seeds, in contrast to the rotating-frame ones. It does not change the underlying scaling: the cost of representing strongly entangled states is untouched and will, we expect, set the practical limit for larger and more densely coupled molecules. Natural next steps are to carry the same idea into p-tVMC, applying the offset evolution exactly and projecting only the coupling, and to replace the dense propagator with a Trotter decomposition.
